title: How do economists approach the world?
summary: Economists build simplified models, test them against evidence and use ceteris paribus. The subject has developed through competing schools of thought and nine key concepts frame the course.

keyterms.definition: A simplified representation of reality, built on assumptions, used to explain and predict economic behaviour.
Latin for "other things being equal"; the assumption that only one variable changes while all others are held constant.
A simplifying condition a model takes as given, e.g. that consumers are rational.
A testable statement about a relationship between variables that can be checked against data.
Information gathered from observation and data, used to test economic theories.
Developing a hypothesis, testing it with data and accepting, revising or rejecting the theory.
A school of thought holding that free markets self-correct and government intervention should be minimal.
A school of thought arguing that economies can stay below full employment and that government spending can raise demand.
A field combining psychology and economics to study why people often do not behave as rational, self-interested maximisers.
The nine ideas framing the course: scarcity, choice, efficiency, equity, economic well-being, sustainability, change, interdependence, intervention.
Making the best use of scarce resources, e.g. producing at lowest cost or allocating resources to what society values most.
Fairness; in economics often about how fairly income, wealth and opportunities are distributed.
Meeting present needs without compromising the ability of future generations to meet theirs.
The level of prosperity, economic security and quality of life people enjoy.

lessons.title: Models, assumptions and the scientific method

questions.prompt: Why do economists use the ceteris paribus assumption?
options: To isolate the effect of one variable on another
To remove the need for data
To show that markets are always efficient
questions.explanation: Holding other factors constant lets economists study a single cause-and-effect relationship.

questions.text: A simplified representation of reality used to explain and predict is an economic ___.
questions.explanation: Models simplify the real world so its key relationships can be analysed.

questions.statement: An economic model is useless if its assumptions are not completely realistic.
questions.explanation: All models simplify. A model is judged by how well it explains and predicts, though unrealistic assumptions can limit it.

questions.prompt: Put the steps of the scientific method in economics in order.
items: Accept, revise or reject the theory
questions.explanation: Economists observe, hypothesise, test against data and then refine theories, although controlled experiments are rarely possible.

options: A 10% rise in the price of cigarettes reduced smoking by 4%
The government should tax cigarettes more heavily
Smoking is a bad habit that must end
It is unfair to tax smokers
questions.explanation: Positive statements can be tested against evidence; the others contain value judgements (normative).

questions.statement: "The minimum wage ought to be raised" is a normative statement.
questions.explanation: "Ought" signals a value judgement that cannot be proven true or false.

questions.prompt: Why is it hard for economists to run controlled experiments?
options: Economies involve many people and variables that cannot be held constant
Economic theories cannot be tested at all
questions.explanation: Economists rely mostly on observed data and natural or field experiments because they cannot control whole economies in a lab.

questions.prompt: Match the term to its meaning.

pairs.right: A simplifying condition taken as given
Data from observation of the real world

questions.explanation: These are the building blocks of how economists construct and test theories.

questions.prompt: An economist finds that data do not support her hypothesis. What should she do according to the scientific method?
options: Assume ceteris paribus was violated and keep the theory unchanged
questions.explanation: Theories that fail empirical tests should be refined or replaced.

questions.text: Studying how psychology causes people to depart from rational choice is ___ economics.
questions.explanation: Behavioural economics brings insights from psychology into economic decision making.

lessons.title: Schools of thought and key concepts

questions.prompt: Which view is most closely associated with Keynesian economics?
options: Markets always clear quickly without intervention
Government spending can lift an economy out of a recession
Only the money supply matters for output
questions.explanation: Keynes argued that deficient demand could leave an economy stuck below full employment, justifying government action.

questions.statement: Classical economists generally believe that the economy tends to move back to full employment on its own.
questions.explanation: Classical (and later monetarist/new classical) thinkers emphasise self-correcting markets through flexible prices and wages.

questions.prompt: Match each key concept to an illustration.

pairs.right: Protecting fish stocks for future catches
Reducing the gap between rich and poor
Producing output at the lowest possible cost
Countries relying on each other through trade

questions.explanation: The nine key concepts give a lens for analysing any economic issue, including in the IA.

questions.text: Fairness in the distribution of income and opportunities is the key concept of ___.
questions.explanation: Equity means fairness, which is not the same as equality (everyone having the same).

questions.prompt: Which pair are BOTH among the nine IB economics key concepts?
questions.explanation: The nine are scarcity, choice, efficiency, equity, economic well-being, sustainability, change, interdependence and intervention.

questions.statement: Equity and equality mean exactly the same thing in economics.
questions.explanation: Equity is about fairness; an equal distribution is not necessarily seen as fair, and a fair one need not be equal.

questions.prompt: The idea that people use rules of thumb and are affected by how choices are framed comes from…
questions.explanation: Behavioural economics studies biases and heuristics in real decision making.

questions.prompt: Order these economic thinkers or ideas by when they became influential, earliest first.
questions.explanation: Smith wrote in 1776, Keynes in the 1930s, monetarism rose in the 1970s and behavioural economics became mainstream from the late 20th century.

questions.prompt: A news article about a city providing free bus passes to low-income residents best fits which key concept?
questions.explanation: Targeting help at low-income households is mainly about fairness, though intervention is also involved.

questions.text: The key concept about meeting present needs without harming future generations is ___.
questions.explanation: Sustainability links environmental and economic choices across time.
